headline: Oil climbs, bond yields fall, and the fear gauge rises
summary: US stocks ended mixed, with the [[Dow]] up 0.33% while the [[Nasdaq]] fell 0.62%, which fits a day when investors kept giving back some of Monday's big AI rally. Nvidia surrendered a large chunk of its gains, and the [[VIX]] rose 7.32% to 28.29, so traders were still paying up for protection even though the S&P 500 only slipped 0.25%. The [[10-year yield]] fell 6 [[basis points]] to 4.85% and the dollar index slipped 0.13%, though it's not obvious why yields dropped. Oil moved the other way, with WTI crude up 1.99% to 83.68 because Middle East tension keeps supply worries alive, and that matters because the Fed's favorite inflation gauge, the [[PCE price index]], already sits at 3.8%. Put together, the market is juggling two worries at once, an AI trade that has lost its footing and an energy-driven inflation problem that makes it hard for central banks to help.
one_thing: Inflation is running at 3.8% while the Fed's rate is only 3.875%, so the [[real interest rate]] is close to zero and policy is hardly tight. That means the 2027 rate cuts that stock investors are counting on look shaky as long as oil keeps climbing.

cross_asset.stocks: The S&P 500 slipped 0.25%, the Nasdaq fell 0.62% and the Dow rose 0.33%, so money tilted away from big tech and toward the rest of the market. The reason is the AI jitters, because Nvidia gave back a big piece of Monday's rally and so much of the index rides on a handful of AI-linked firms. Oracle and CoreWeave sank early and then bounced, so the day was bumpy but ended less ugly than it began.
cross_asset.rates: The 10-year yield fell 6 basis points to 4.85%, which is a decent one-day move (6 basis points is 0.06 percentage points). The headlines don't say why, though a bit of safe-haven buying while tech wobbled would fit. The catch is that inflation at 3.8% leaves little room for yields to fall much further, because bond buyers want to be paid more than inflation.
cross_asset.fx: The dollar index slipped 0.13% to 103.67, which continues the fade from its 20-month high, and lower Treasury yields make holding dollars a little less rewarding. USD/JPY rose 0.16% to 159.26, so the yen stayed weak because Japan's 1.25% rate sits 2.625 percentage points below the Fed's 3.875%. Japan has already stepped in to buy yen with a record $50 billion in one day, so traders keep a close eye on any further push toward higher USD/JPY.
cross_asset.commodities: WTI crude rose 1.99% to 83.68, its second straight gain, because Middle East tension is outweighing expectations for a global supply surplus. Gold fell 0.73% to 3535.8, which is a little odd since lower yields and a softer dollar usually help gold, and the cause isn't clear. Higher oil is the bigger story for the broad market, because it feeds straight into inflation.

storylines.name: Central banks vs energy inflation
storylines.backstory: The Iran war cut oil supply and pushed up [[headline inflation]], so central banks have been trying to decide whether the price jump fades on its own or leaks into wages and services. Euro area inflation reached 4%, the Bank of England hiked to 4%, and the Fed sits at 3.875%.
storylines.today: The PCE price index rose 3.8% from a year earlier in October, matching forecasts, and third quarter [[GDP]] was revised up to 4.3%, so the economy is strong while prices are hot. That leaves the Fed's rate barely above inflation, and a CNBC commentary argues that Kevin Warsh should hike instead of betting on a productivity boom the way Greenspan did. The ECB's account of its October meeting adds that energy prices pushed oil and gas above its own adverse scenario, and markets at one point priced in more than four extra hikes before settling on just under three. Households are feeling it too, with even toys getting pricier and holiday budgets shrinking.
storylines.market_link: Oil stays high, which keeps headline inflation near 3.8%, so central banks can't promise cuts and may even have to hike. Because rate cuts are what investors hoped would lift 2027 company earnings, that hope fades, and stocks that are expensive relative to earnings come under pressure. At the same time, strong growth and sticky inflation keep bond yields high, which makes mortgages and business loans cost more.
storylines.next_chapter: A hotter inflation report, a hawkish speech from a Fed official, or a clearer signal from Warsh about hiking would push the story forward. A fall in oil would do the opposite and let central banks relax.
note: The big idea is that the Fed's preferred inflation gauge is 3.8% and its rate is 3.875%, so after inflation the Fed is barely charging anything for money.
The cause is the Iran war pushing up energy costs, and the worry is that those costs leak into wages and services, which would make inflation last.
The so-what is that stock investors counting on rate cuts in 2027 may be disappointed, and the next debate is whether the Fed hikes instead.
Interview line: inflation is a supply problem on top of strong demand, so the Fed has almost no room to ease.

storylines.name: Iran war and oil
storylines.backstory: The conflict began in early 2026 and cut global oil output by 12 million barrels a day in March, but prices stayed below records because stored oil filled the gap. The IEA says the Hormuz shock lifted the world's oil and gas import bill 25% to $1.6 trillion, and pump prices recently fell to their lowest level since March.
storylines.today: WTI crude rose 1.99% to 83.68, its second straight gain, because tension in the Middle East outweighed expectations for a global supply surplus. The ECB's account of its October meeting says freight rates from the Gulf to Europe hit record highs, diesel [[crack spreads]] sit above the levels after Russia's 2022 invasion, and the odds of a US-Iran peace deal by the end of 2026 were the lowest since the war began. Meanwhile the UAE says it expects 7% to 8% growth next year as the IMF lifts its forecast, which shows that the Gulf is coping better than the headlines might suggest.
storylines.market_link: Oil gets more expensive, which raises the cost of fuel and shipping, so businesses pay more and pass some of it on to shoppers. That pushes inflation up, which keeps central banks from cutting rates, so bond yields stay high and stock valuations feel pressure. Households then cut back on gifts, travel and food, which slows spending.
storylines.next_chapter: Any sign of a US-Iran peace deal would likely pull oil down quickly, while a worse Gulf shipping disruption would send prices higher. A real global supply surplus showing up would also cap the rally.
note: The big idea is that oil is rising again because the war keeps supply fragile, even though prices are well below record highs.
Stored oil filled the gap earlier, but that cushion doesn't last forever, which is why tension can still push WTI up about 2% in a day.
Diesel and shipping costs are rising even faster than crude, which means businesses feel the pain before drivers do.
Interview line: oil is the first domino, because it moves inflation, then central banks, then bond yields.

storylines.name: AI trade jitters
storylines.backstory: The biggest AI-linked tech firms hold up so much of the S&P 500 that doubts about AI hit the whole market. Nvidia's CEO left on Nov 12, a selloff followed, official papers warned that AI [[valuation]]s look stretched, and the index fell four straight weeks. Then Nvidia's board approved Huang's return and the Nasdaq jumped 6.51% on Monday.
storylines.today: Nvidia gave back a big chunk of Monday's rally, and according to Vanda Research the gains of retail investors who bought the dip last week are now nearly all gone. Oracle and CoreWeave sank early and then bounced, so the day ended less ugly than it began. Vance said he was assured Huang was not under a DOJ investigation, while a CNBC column says Treasury Secretary Bessent's about-face on Huang shows how unsettled the administration's stance on Nvidia and China is. The ECB's account of its October meeting also lists worries about the increasingly debt-financed AI investment cycle.
storylines.market_link: Nvidia and its AI peers are such a large slice of the index that when they fall, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq fall with them. Falling tech prices make investors nervous, which lifts the VIX and can push money toward safer assets like Treasuries. If AI spending is being paid for with borrowed money, higher yields make that borrowing more expensive, which adds another source of stress.
storylines.next_chapter: Clearer news on Huang, the administration's stance on Nvidia and China, or a fresh AI earnings surprise would move the story. Another jump in yields would also hurt, because expensive tech stocks are the most sensitive to higher rates.
note: The big idea is that the market has become so dependent on a few AI firms that one wobbly stock can drag down the entire index.
The Monday rally faded quickly, which suggests the relief came from a headline and not from a real change in the AI outlook.
The so-what is that when AI stocks and inflation worries hit at once, investors get hit from both sides, because rates stay high and the biggest stocks get cheaper.
Interview line: the Dow held up better than the Nasdaq today, which shows how much of the pain sits in tech.

storylines.name: US midterms and the dollar
storylines.backstory: The midterms produced what headlines call a Democratic rout, and markets asked how divided government might change tariffs, spending and the dollar. The dollar then had its biggest rally since 2024, with headlines crediting hawkish Fed bets and not the election, and it hit a 20-month high, its strongest since March 2025.
storylines.today: The dollar index slipped 0.13% to 103.67 as Treasury yields fell, and commentary now suggests the dollar may be peaking. The US also announced plans for new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU, and the Swiss franc gained as a safe haven. Tuesday's consumer confidence reading jumped to 103.3 after the Democratic wins, though inflation worries persist.
storylines.market_link: A dollar rises when US yields are higher than elsewhere, because investors want to hold the currency that pays more. When yields fall, that reason weakens, so the dollar slips, and a weaker dollar makes imports pricier for Americans but helps US exporters. Safe-haven buying of the Swiss franc shows some investors are choosing safety over return.
storylines.next_chapter: A move higher in Treasury yields would give the dollar new support, while more tariff news or a dovish turn at the Fed would add to the case that the peak is behind us.
note: The big idea is that the dollar's post-election rally looks tired, with the index down at 103.67 after hitting a 20-month high.
The reason is that the rally came from hawkish Fed bets and not from the election itself, so when yields fall the dollar loses its main support.
The so-what is that a fading dollar eases pressure on emerging markets and commodities priced in dollars, while the yen still struggles against a Fed rate far above Japan's.
Consumer confidence jumping is a nice headline, but the St. Louis Fed says it predicts spending only weakly.

stories.title: The Fed's favorite inflation gauge leaves it little room
stories.what: The PCE price index rose 3.8% from a year earlier in October, exactly what forecasters expected, and third quarter GDP was revised up to 4.3%. The Fed's rate is 3.875%, so it sits only slightly above inflation.
stories.why: When growth is strong and inflation is high, a central bank can't cut rates without risking even higher prices. Because a rate that is barely above inflation isn't very restrictive, hiking becomes a real option, which is what the CNBC commentary on Warsh argues.
stories.watch: Any Fed comment about rates possibly rising, and whether the next inflation reports come in hotter or cooler than 3.8%.

stories.title: Oil rises again on Middle East tension
stories.what: WTI crude gained 1.99% to 83.68, its second straight gain. Tension in the Middle East outweighed expectations for a supply surplus.
stories.why: Higher oil raises costs for fuel, shipping and food, which feeds into the inflation numbers central banks watch. It also hits households directly, with CNBC noting that toys, food and travel are all getting more expensive as people scale back holiday plans.
stories.watch: News on US-Iran peace talks, since the ECB's account says the odds of a deal by the end of 2026 are the lowest since the war began.

stories.title: Tech slips and the VIX climbs
stories.what: The Nasdaq fell 0.62% and the VIX rose 7.32% to 28.29, while the Dow gained 0.33%. Nvidia gave back a large part of Monday's rally.
stories.why: A VIX near 28 means traders expect large swings and are paying more for protection. Because AI-linked firms are so large in the index, any doubt about them spreads to the whole market.
stories.watch: Whether Nvidia stabilizes, and any news about Huang and the administration's stance on Nvidia and China.

stories.title: The yen stays weak near 159 per dollar
stories.what: USD/JPY rose 0.16% to 159.26. The BOJ chief played down soft consumption data and signaled a near-term rate hike, while Japan's inflation accelerated and its economy unexpectedly shrank in the third quarter.
stories.why: The BOJ's 1.25% rate is 2.625 percentage points below the Fed's 3.875%, so investors earn more by selling yen and holding dollars. Japan's energy costs rise with oil, which hurts its trade balance and adds more pressure on the yen.
stories.watch: Whether the BOJ actually hikes, and whether Japan steps in again to buy yen after its record $50 billion intervention.

stories.title: Consumers feel better but are still cutting back
stories.what: Consumer confidence jumped to 103.3 after the Democratic midterm wins, while CNBC reports that Americans are scaling back holiday plans because of higher prices.
stories.why: A St. Louis Fed piece finds that consumer confidence has only a small ability to predict spending, and that the change in unemployment has roughly 10 times the effect. So a good survey result doesn't guarantee that people will actually spend more.
stories.watch: Actual holiday spending and the jobs data, which matter more than surveys.

under_the_radar.title: America's shrinking labor supply
under_the_radar.what: A New York Fed post says growth in the US working-age population has fallen to near zero after a sharp drop in net immigration, and the available labor supply could soon begin to shrink. Other advanced economies have already been through this, and many of them kept their labor forces growing by getting more women and people aged 65 to 74 into work.
under_the_radar.chain: Fewer available workers makes hiring harder, so companies may need to pay more to keep staff. Higher wages push up the cost of services, which means inflation can stay high even if oil prices calm down, so central banks would have to keep rates higher for longer and bond yields would stay elevated.
under_the_radar.watch: Wage growth in the jobs reports and whether the share of people in the labor force keeps rising.
note: The big idea is that the US is running out of new workers, because immigration has dropped and the native-born working-age group is shrinking.
This matters because central banks are asking whether the oil price jump leaks into wages, and a tight labor market is exactly what would make that happen.
Other rich countries kept their workforces growing by raising participation, so the US may be able to do the same, but that takes time.
Interview line: the labor supply story is how an energy shock turns into lasting inflation.

under_the_radar.title: Companies lean harder on bond markets
under_the_radar.what: A New York Fed post says US nonfinancial corporate bonds were 29% of US GDP at the end of 2024, and that growth in bond markets can come either from firms borrowing more in general or from firms shifting away from banks. The distinction matters because credit conditions in the bond market and at banks can be disconnected.
under_the_radar.chain: If firms depend more on bonds, then moves in bond yields and [[credit spreads]] matter more for their funding costs. With the 10-year yield at 4.85%, refinancing is expensive, and if stocks keep wobbling investors may demand more extra yield from riskier companies, which would make borrowing harder and could slow hiring and investment.
under_the_radar.watch: A widening in credit spreads or a pause in new bond sales by companies.
note: The big idea is that companies borrow from two places, banks and bond investors, and the mix matters for how fast stress spreads.
If firms simply borrow more of everything, they are exposed to both markets, and if they swap bank loans for bonds, they are more exposed to market mood.
The so-what is that a nervous market can tighten funding for companies even if banks are still lending.
Interview line: I'd watch credit spreads, because they show whether stock volatility is leaking into corporate funding.

under_the_radar.title: Bowman says supervisors must act on what they know
under_the_radar.what: Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman, speaking by video to a Brazil meeting of bank supervisors, said the Silicon Valley Bank failure was not about missing information, because supervisors saw its interest rate risk, concentrated uninsured deposits and weak liquidity planning. The failure, she said, came from not turning that information into timely action.
under_the_radar.chain: Interest rate risk is the danger of losing money on bonds when yields rise, and with the 10-year yield at 4.85% that risk is still very real. A supervision push for earlier action could make weaker banks hold more safety cushions, which could tighten lending a bit and matter for credit conditions.
under_the_radar.watch: Any follow-up from the Fed's independent review of SVB and any sign of stress at banks with large uninsured deposits.
note: The big idea is that the Fed's top bank supervisor wants regulators to act faster, not just collect more data.
The SVB lesson is that a bank with long bonds, uninsured deposits and thin liquidity is fragile when yields rise.
The so-what is that high yields today keep these old risks relevant, and stricter supervision could slow bank lending.
Interview line: SVB was a failure to act on known risks, not a failure to see them.

deep_dive.why_now: The ECB's account of its October meeting shows how a central bank is reacting to the same energy shock hitting the US, and it explains why European rates matter for global markets.
key_points: Energy pressures intensified after the September meeting, with oil and gas prices moving above the ECB staff's adverse scenario, and diesel refining margins and Gulf freight rates reaching historic highs.
Inflation fixings, which are market bets on future inflation, peaked at 4.5% for January 2027 and stayed above 2.5% until the first quarter of 2028.

Even so, expectations for ECB rates stayed near September levels, because markets understood that rates would not move in lockstep with energy costs. Pricing implied a peak deposit rate around 3%, which is higher than the one more hike that surveyed analysts expected.

Longer euro area rates rose mainly because of higher real term premia, which reflect uncertainty and a growing supply of public and private debt, and stocks and bonds have started moving together more often, so bonds protect portfolios less.
Markets are also worried about fiscal dynamics and the increasingly debt-financed AI investment cycle.
deep_dive.market_angle: Euro area short-term rates are sensitive to oil and gas news, so higher energy prices push them up and a peace deal would pull them down. Long yields on both sides of the Atlantic are being driven by debt supply and uncertainty, which means they can rise even when central banks hold still. Stocks and bonds falling together would hurt balanced portfolios.
deep_dive.trade_idea: A desk might receive euro short-term swap rates, betting that markets price more ECB hikes than the one that surveyed analysts expect. The main risk is that oil and gas keep rising, which would force the ECB to turn more hawkish and make the trade lose money.
note: The big idea is that the ECB sees the energy shock as serious, but it has signaled it won't automatically hike every time energy prices rise.
Markets are pricing about three more hikes at one point, while analysts only expect one, so there is a gap between traders and forecasters.
Long yields are rising for reasons beyond central banks, namely uncertainty and a growing pile of debt to be sold.
Interview line: when stocks and bonds fall together, bonds stop being a safe hedge, which is a big problem for portfolios.
deep_dive.title: Meeting of 28-29 October 2026

deep_dive.why_now: With oil driving inflation higher, this San Francisco Fed letter helps explain why Fed moves may not push long-term yields the way many people expect.
key_points: The Fed tends to react more aggressively to demand-driven inflation, where prices and quantities rise together, than to supply-driven inflation, where prices rise while quantities fall.
The authors look at policy surprises, meaning the unexpected part of Fed announcements, and how they change forward rates, which are what the market expects interest rates to be in the future.
Surprises mostly pass through to longer-horizon forward rates when inflation is demand-driven.
Supply-driven inflation tends to follow food and energy prices, so with supply pressures back, Fed surprises are likely to have a smaller effect on longer-horizon yields.
deep_dive.market_angle: Short-term Treasury yields should still react to Fed news, but 10-year yields may respond less and instead follow term premium, debt supply and inflation worries. So a hawkish Fed surprise could lift 2-year yields more than 10-year yields, which flattens the curve.
deep_dive.trade_idea: A desk might position for 2-year yields to move more than 10-year yields around Fed news, which is a curve flattener if the Fed turns hawkish. The main risk is that rising debt supply or inflation fears push long yields higher on their own and steepen the curve instead.
note: The big idea is that where inflation comes from changes how much the Fed's moves matter for long-term interest rates.

Demand inflation means too much spending, and the Fed's response travels through the whole yield curve, while supply inflation like an oil shock gives the Fed a messier choice and a weaker effect on long yields.
The so-what is that mortgage rates, which follow long yields, may not move as much as people expect even if the Fed acts.
Interview line: this oil shock is a supply shock, so I'd expect the front end of the curve to react more to the Fed than the 10-year does.

terms.def: It's the Fed's favorite inflation gauge, like a grocery receipt that tracks how much the typical family's basket of spending costs compared with a year ago.
It's the interest rate minus inflation, like a savings account paying 4% when prices rise 3.8%, which leaves you with almost no real gain.
It's a fear gauge that shows how much traders expect stocks to swing, like an insurance price that rises when storm clouds gather.
It's the extra yield investors ask for to lock money in a long bond, like a bonus you want for lending to someone for ten years instead of one.
It's a sudden drop in how much of something is available, like a flood that wipes out a harvest and pushes up the price of bread.
It's the extra yield a riskier borrower pays over the government, like the higher rate a friend with a shaky job would pay on a car loan.

cross_asset_notes: The big idea of the day is that markets are caught between an AI trade that is wobbling and an energy-driven inflation problem that won't go away.
Oil rose 1.99% to 83.68, which keeps inflation high, so the Fed can't promise cuts, and that is why the hope for 2027 earnings looks fragile.
The 10-year yield fell 6 basis points to 4.85% and the dollar slipped, but the headlines don't explain why, so it would be a mistake to read it as a clear sign that inflation fears are easing.
The VIX rose 7.32% to 28.29 even though the S&P 500 only fell 0.25%, which shows that traders are nervous beneath a calm-looking index.
Interview line: oil is pushing inflation up while AI doubts hit stocks, so rates stay high and the biggest stocks have less cushion.
take: Inflation is 3.8%, the Fed's rate is 3.875%, oil is climbing and the 10-year Treasury yield sits at 4.85%. Would you buy or sell the 10-year Treasury here, and what would prove you wrong?

10-year yield.def: It's the interest rate the US government pays to borrow money for ten years. It also helps set the rates on mortgages and business loans.
10-year yield.analogy: It's like the interest rate on a ten-year loan you make to the government.
10-year yield.today: The 10-year yield fell 6 basis points to 4.85%, and the headlines don't explain why.

Dow.def: The Dow is an index that tracks 30 large, well-known US companies. It leans toward industrial and traditional firms more than the Nasdaq does.
Dow.analogy: It's like a report card for 30 of the biggest names in American business.
Dow.today: The Dow rose 0.33% to 50182.95 while tech stocks fell, which shows money tilting away from the AI names.

GDP.def: GDP is the total value of everything an economy produces in a period. It's the broadest scorecard for how fast an economy is growing.
GDP.analogy: It's like the total sales figure for an entire country.
GDP.today: Third quarter GDP was revised up to 4.3%, so the economy is strong even while prices run hot.

Nasdaq.def: The Nasdaq is an index packed with technology and growth companies. It tends to swing more than the broader market when tech stocks move.
Nasdaq.analogy: It's like a team made mostly of star players, so it wins big and loses big.
Nasdaq.today: The Nasdaq fell 0.62% to 23585.8 as Nvidia gave back a big piece of Monday's rally.

PCE price index.def: It's the Fed's favorite measure of inflation, tracking how much the prices of what households buy have changed over a year.
PCE price index.analogy: It's like a grocery receipt for the whole economy, compared with the same receipt a year ago.
PCE price index.today: It rose 3.8% from a year earlier in October, exactly what forecasters expected.

VIX.def: The VIX measures how much traders expect US stocks to swing over the next month. A higher number means more fear and more demand for protection.
VIX.analogy: It's like the price of storm insurance, which rises when dark clouds gather.
VIX.today: The VIX rose 7.32% to 28.29, so traders stayed nervous even though the S&P 500 only slipped 0.25%.

basis points.def: A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, and traders use it to describe small changes in interest rates.
basis points.analogy: It's like measuring a short walk in inches instead of miles.
basis points.today: The 10-year yield fell 6 basis points, which is 0.06 percentage points.

crack spreads.def: A crack spread is the gap between the price of a refined fuel like diesel and the price of the crude oil used to make it. A wide gap means refiners are earning big margins and fuel is costly.
crack spreads.analogy: It's like the markup between the price of flour and the price of the finished loaf of bread.
crack spreads.today: Euro area diesel crack spreads sit above the levels seen after Russia's 2022 invasion, so businesses feel fuel costs even faster than crude shows.

credit spreads.def: A credit spread is the extra yield a riskier company pays compared with the government. It widens when investors get nervous about lending to companies.
credit spreads.analogy: It's like the higher interest rate a friend with a shaky job would pay on a car loan.
credit spreads.today: Credit spreads are worth watching because a nervous stock market could leak into company borrowing costs.

headline inflation.def: Headline inflation is the overall rise in prices, including food and energy, which swing a lot. Central banks also watch a narrower measure that leaves those out.
headline inflation.analogy: It's like the full price on your receipt before anyone takes out the items that jump around.
headline inflation.today: Oil's climb keeps headline inflation near 3.8%, which is why the Fed can't promise cuts.

real interest rate.def: The real interest rate is a normal interest rate minus inflation. It shows how much a lender really earns or how tight policy really is once rising prices are counted.
real interest rate.analogy: It's like a savings account paying 4% when prices rise 3.8%, so you gain almost nothing.
real interest rate.today: The Fed's 3.875% rate against 3.8% inflation leaves a real rate near zero, so policy is hardly tight.

valuation.def: Valuation describes how expensive a stock is compared with what the company earns. A high valuation means investors are paying a lot for each dollar of profit.
valuation.analogy: It's like paying $50 for a lemonade stand that earns $1 a year, which only works if you expect it to grow a lot.
valuation.today: AI valuations look stretched, so when Nvidia fell the whole market felt it.

steps.label: Middle East tension
steps.explain: Fighting and shipping risk in the Middle East keep oil supply fragile.
steps.detail: The Iran war cut global output earlier this year, and stored oil has been filling the gap. Odds of a US-Iran peace deal are the lowest since the war began, so supply worries stay alive.

steps.label: WTI crude rises
steps.explain: Oil gained 1.99% to 83.68, its second straight rise.
steps.detail: Traders are weighing tension against expectations for a global supply surplus, and today tension won. A 2% move in a day is a clear signal that the supply cushion is thinning.

steps.label: Business costs climb
steps.explain: Dearer oil makes fuel and shipping more expensive for companies.
steps.detail: Diesel refining margins are historically high and freight from the Gulf to Europe hit record highs. Businesses then pass some of those costs on to shoppers, which is why even toys are getting pricier.

steps.label: Inflation stays hot
steps.explain: Higher costs keep prices rising near 3.8% a year.
steps.detail: The Fed's favorite gauge, the [[PCE price index]], rose 3.8% in October. Oil keeps [[headline inflation]] from cooling, so the number is hard to bring down.

steps.label: Fed can't promise cuts
steps.explain: Central banks have little room to lower rates while prices rise this fast.
steps.detail: Investors hoped for rate cuts to lift 2027 company profits. With inflation this high, that hope looks shaky, and stocks that are expensive compared with earnings come under pressure.

steps.label: Inflation at 3.8%
steps.explain: The Fed's preferred gauge matched forecasts at 3.8% for October.
steps.detail: There was no surprise in the number, but it lands while third quarter [[GDP]] was revised up to 4.3%. Strong growth plus hot prices is a tough mix for a central bank.

steps.label: Fed rate barely higher
steps.explain: The Fed's rate is 3.875%, only a hair above inflation.
steps.detail: Subtract inflation from the rate and the [[real interest rate]] is close to zero. In other words, the Fed is hardly charging anything after prices are counted.

steps.label: Policy looks loose
steps.explain: A near-zero real rate means money isn't really tight.
steps.detail: That is why a CNBC commentary argues Kevin Warsh should hike instead of betting on a productivity boom the way Greenspan did. Hiking is now a real option, not just a thought experiment.

steps.label: Yields stay high
steps.explain: The 10-year yield sat at 4.85% after falling 6 basis points.
steps.detail: Bond buyers want to be paid more than inflation, so yields can't fall much with prices rising 3.8%. The headlines don't explain today's dip, so it's not a clear sign that worries are easing.

steps.label: Borrowing stays costly
steps.explain: High yields keep mortgages and business loans expensive.
steps.detail: Long-term loan rates follow the 10-year yield, so households and companies don't get relief. That slows spending and hiring over time.

steps.label: Nvidia gives back gains
steps.explain: Nvidia lost a big chunk of Monday's rally.
steps.detail: Monday's jump came after Nvidia's board approved Huang's return, which was a headline and not a real change in the AI outlook. Retail investors who bought last week's dip have now given up nearly all their gains.

steps.label: Nasdaq slides
steps.explain: The Nasdaq fell 0.62% because it holds so many AI-linked firms.
steps.detail: A handful of AI companies make up a big slice of the index. So doubts about them hit the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 even when other stocks are fine.

steps.label: Fear gauge jumps
steps.explain: The VIX rose 7.32% to 28.29 as traders bought protection.
steps.detail: A [[VIX]] near 28 means traders expect big swings. That's a sign of nerves under a calm-looking S&P 500, which only fell 0.25%.

steps.label: Money rotates
steps.explain: Investors leaned toward the rest of the market instead of tech.
steps.detail: The Dow rose 0.33% while the Nasdaq fell, which shows the pain sat in tech. Oracle and CoreWeave sank early and then bounced, so the day ended less ugly than it began.

quiz.q: The Dow rose 0.33% while the Nasdaq fell 0.62%. What best explains the gap?
options: Nvidia gave back much of Monday's rally, and tech weighs more
Consumer confidence jumped, which pulled money out of tech
Oil fell, which helped industrial firms in the Dow more
The 10-year yield rose, which hurt tech stocks the most
quiz.explain: Nvidia surrendered a large part of Monday's gains and AI-linked firms are a big share of the Nasdaq. Oil actually rose and the 10-year yield fell, so those two options get the facts backwards.

quiz.q: The VIX rose 7.32% to 28.29, which means traders kept paying up for protection even though the S&P 500 slipped only 0.25%.
options: True
False
quiz.explain: A rising VIX shows demand for protection. The calm-looking index hides nerves underneath, mostly tied to the AI selloff.

quiz.q: The 10-year yield fell 6 basis points to 4.85%, and the headlines clearly credit safe-haven buying for the drop.
options: True
False
quiz.explain: The headlines don't explain the drop. Safe-haven buying would fit while tech wobbled, but it isn't confirmed.

quiz.q: A US-Iran peace deal is signed, and Gulf shipping risk fades. What would WTI crude probably do?
options: Up
Down
quiz.explain: Odds of a deal are the lowest since the war began, so a deal would remove much of the supply worry that lifted WTI to 83.68. Prices would likely drop quickly.

quiz.q: The Bank of Japan hikes soon, as its chief signaled, and the rate gap with the Fed narrows. What would USD/JPY probably do from 159.26?
options: Up
Down
quiz.explain: The yen is weak because Japan's 1.25% rate sits 2.625 points under the Fed's 3.875%. A smaller gap makes holding yen less costly, so USD/JPY would likely fall.

quiz.q: Diesel and Gulf freight costs jump further, so inflation worries grow. What would the 10-year yield probably do from 4.85%?
options: Up
Down
quiz.explain: Many assume a scare means bond buying and lower yields. But with inflation already at 3.8%, bond buyers demand more yield and the Fed has less room to cut, so yields would likely rise.

quiz.q: Put today's oil chain in the right order, from cause to effect.
items: Middle East tension lifts WTI crude
Fuel and shipping costs rise for businesses
The Fed has less room to cut rates
quiz.explain: Oil moves first, then business costs, then inflation, and only then does the central bank's room to cut shrink.

quiz.q: Order the steps that put a Fed hike on the table.
items: Fed rate of 3.875% is barely above it
Commentators argue the Fed may need to hike
quiz.explain: The gap between inflation and the policy rate is what makes policy look loose, and that is the basis for the hike argument.

quiz.q: The PCE price index is 3.8% and the Fed's rate is 3.875%. Why does that matter?
options: Policy is very tight, so cuts are likely to start soon
Policy is very loose, so the Fed has to cut right away
Inflation is below the rate, so bond yields must now fall
Policy is barely tight, so a hike becomes a real debate
quiz.explain: A rate only slightly above inflation leaves a real rate near zero. That makes hiking a live option and makes cuts look unlikely.

quiz.q: USD/JPY rose 0.16% to 159.26 even after Japan's record $50 billion intervention. What best explains the weak yen?
options: The BOJ chief ruled out any hike, so yen traders gave up
Japan's rate is far below the Fed's, so holding yen pays less
Japan's economy grew in Q3, so investors bought more yen
Japan ran a trade surplus again, so demand for yen stayed firm
quiz.explain: Japan's economy actually shrank in Q3, it ran a sixth straight trade deficit, and the BOJ chief signaled a near-term hike. The rate gap with the Fed is what keeps pushing investors toward dollars.

quiz.q: Gold fell 0.73% while the 10-year yield fell and the dollar slipped. Which reading fits?
options: Surprising, because oil rose and gold always follows oil up
Normal, because higher oil always pushes gold lower
Normal, because lower yields and a softer dollar hurt gold
Surprising, because lower yields and a softer dollar help gold
quiz.explain: Lower yields and a weaker dollar usually help gold, so the drop is odd and the cause isn't clear. Gold doesn't mechanically follow oil in either direction.

quiz.q: The dollar index slipped 0.13% to 103.67. What best explains the move?
options: Hawkish Fed bets surged, which cut demand for dollars
The midterm wins weakened the currency right away
Lower Treasury yields made holding dollars pay a bit less
Consumer confidence jumped, which reduced demand for dollars
quiz.explain: The dollar's earlier rally came from hawkish Fed bets, not from the election. With yields falling, its main support weakened and commentary now suggests the dollar may be peaking.

quiz.q: The San Francisco Fed letter finds the Fed reacts more strongly to supply-driven inflation than to demand-driven inflation.
options: True
False
quiz.explain: It's the reverse. The Fed tends to respond more aggressively to demand-driven inflation, so surprises pass through to long yields less when inflation comes from supply shocks like oil.

quiz.q: Why does the New York Fed's note on a shrinking US labor supply matter for the inflation debate?
options: Immigration only matters for stocks, not for central banks
Fewer workers lowers wages, so services inflation cools
Fewer workers could lift wages, so the oil shock sticks
More workers could lift wages, so the oil shock fades
quiz.explain: Central banks worry that energy costs leak into wages and services. A tight labor market is exactly what would let that happen and keep inflation high even if oil calms.

quiz.q: Fed Vice Chair Bowman said supervisors spotted Silicon Valley Bank's main weaknesses but failed to act on them in time.
options: True
False
quiz.explain: Her point was that the failure was not a lack of information, since interest rate risk, uninsured deposits and weak liquidity were visible. The failure was not turning that into timely action.

quiz.q: The ECB's account says euro area 10-year rates rose mainly because of what?
options: Central banks promised hikes each time oil prices rose
Higher real term premia from uncertainty and growing debt supply
Higher expected inflation alone, which explains nearly all of it
Investors piled into bonds as AI stocks wobbled
quiz.explain: The ECB said higher real term premia drove most of the rise, while higher expected short-term rates and inflation explained only about a third. That's why long yields can climb even when central banks hold still.
